report:
## Conclusion

The claim that drinking boiled garlic water cures COVID-19 is **false**. There is no clinical evidence that garlic — boiled, raw, or in any preparation — can cure, treat, or prevent COVID-19 in humans. This myth spread widely early in the pandemic and has been repeatedly debunked by international fact-checkers and health authorities, including the World Health Organization, which explicitly states garlic "has some antimicrobial properties" but "there is no evidence from the current outbreak that eating garlic has protected people from the new coronavirus" (AFP Fact Check, Rappler).

Some laboratory (in vitro/computational) studies have found that certain garlic-derived compounds can interfere with SARS-CoV-2's spike protein or its ability to bind host-cell receptors, suggesting theoretical antiviral potential. However, these are preliminary, non-clinical findings from petri-dish or modeling experiments, not evidence that drinking garlic water works in real patients. Researchers themselves caution that "further preclinical validation" and human trials are needed before any therapeutic claims can be made (MDPI/PMC studies).

Health professionals warn that relying on garlic water instead of proven medical care is risky, as it may delay appropriate treatment for a potentially serious illness (AFP Fact Check; Groeat). No regulatory or public health body — WHO, CDC, or national health ministries — has endorsed garlic as a treatment or cure for COVID-19.

**Bottom line:** Boiled garlic water has no proven ability to cure COVID-19. While garlic may have general immune-supportive or antimicrobial properties and shows modest antiviral activity in early lab research, it is not a substitute for vaccination, antiviral medication, or medical care.
